wa_mount_rainier_tahoma_glacier.approach: From the Westside Road gate at Dry Creek Trailhead: Tahoma Creek Trail to the Wonderland Trail (~5,600 ft), then onto the southern side of the Tahoma Glacier.
wa_mount_rainier_tahoma_glacier.beta: Grade II-III alpine glacier route. Approach via Westside Road to Tahoma Creek Trail, ascending Wonderland Trail to ~5,600 ft, then climbing southern side of glacier with multiple diagonal traverses.

wa_mount_adams_north_ridge.descent_text: Most parties descend the South Climb to Cold Springs (requiring a car shuttle) because it's faster and lower-angle. Reversing the North Ridge is possible but involves down-climbing sustained steep snow. Watch crevasses on any glacier descent.

wa_mount_shuksan_price_glacier.descent_text: The standard descent is NOT back to the Ruth Creek car — it's over the top and down the Fisher Chimneys to Lake Ann, a completely different trailhead. From the summit pyramid, downclimb and rappel the gully system on the pyramid's west side: climbers typically make 1–3 short rappels off natural anchors (slings on rock horns, occasionally pickets left in snow — don't count on finding a picket anchor still in place) on a single 60 m rope, which doubled through the anchor gives rappels of about 30 m, to drop through the soft or icy sections of the gully, though capable parties often downclimb the whole thing instead. This puts you on Hell's Highway, a ~60 m step of steep snow/alpine ice that accesses the Sulphide Glacier. Cross the Upper Curtis Glacier (watch for opening crevasses and weakening snow bridges by late summer) and downclimb Winnie's Slide, a short ice/snow step that some parties rappel (~30 m) when it's icy or the snow beneath is soft, to reach the top of the Fisher Chimneys. The Chimneys themselves (class 3–4) are generally downclimbed rather than rappelled. Continue down through the chimneys to Lake Ann and out the Lake Ann Trail to the Mount Baker Highway/Artist Point trailhead — roughly 13 miles of trail from where your car is parked at Ruth Creek, so plan a shuttle, hitch, or stashed bike. An alternative is to instead descend the Sulphide Glacier all the way down toward the Baker Lake/Shannon Ridge side — a non-technical glacier walk-off with no rappelling required — but that exits at yet another trailhead, again requiring a car shuttle. Ski parties sometimes reverse the Price Glacier itself (skiing the Price Headwall and the glacier's eastern lobe back to Price Lake), but that is a specialized, avalanche- and icefall-exposed line, not the climbers' descent.

wa_mount_shuksan_white_salmon_glacier.beta: Grade II glacier route with short steep steps: Winnie's Slide is 40-45 degree snow for a few hundred feet and can turn icy late in the season. Above it the line joins the Fisher Chimneys route across the Upper Curtis Glacier. High exposure with steep glacier headwall. Active Hanging Glacier avalanches. Bergschrunds, short steep snow or ice steps, crevasses.

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.beta: Grade: 4th class YDS, AI2-3 ice, M1b mixed, PG-13. Technical: 3,000 ft vertical gain over 5 pitches on the ridge itself. Hazards: Extremely loose and unstable rock (especially late season), bergschrunds, extensive crevassing, icefall terrain. Route: Ascend Ptarmigan Ridge Trail to Camp Kiser, cross Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers northeastward, climb low-moderate snow ramps to ridge at ~7,500 ft, bypass Cockscomb Tower on left via steep snow, continue ridge to summit. Descent: Coleman-Deming Route (easy-moderate glacier). Required: Ice climbing competency, crevasse rescue skills, glacier travel experience, rock scrambling ability. Protection: Few ice screws/pickets, glacier gear essential. Best season: Spring or early summer (late season loose rock creates high hazard). First ascent: July 4, 1961 (Murley, Musser, Vielbig).
wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.fa: Chuck Murley, John Musser, and E. Vielbig, July 4, 1961 (first complete ascent of the ridge)

wa_forbidden_peak_north_ridge.beta: Grade III, 5.6 on the ridge. From Boston Basin high camp, traverse glacier to Sharkfin Col via 10 feet of 5.7 rock and 200 feet of Class 3 gully. Northeast ridge route at ~7,700 ft to summit. Moderate to good granite, high exposure with wonderful ridge position. Glaciers: Quien Sabe Glacier, Boston Glacier.

wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_rib_1.beta: Two start variations exist: the original 1951 Route, which is faster but includes a 'scary' 5.7 pitch, and a 1957 variation that starts lower and adds roughly 500 ft of climbing on more logical terrain to avoid it. From the start, initial 4th-class terrain leads into dense vertical tree-root climbing, a slabby ~60-ft horizontal gully traverse (5.5) with minimal protection, and steep heather sections requiring careful, finger-pressing technique. A roughly 700-ft crux section of higher-quality 5.6 rock climbing leads toward a bivy site near the glacier, two pitches below the summit.
wa_johannesburg_mountain_northeast_rib_1.overview: A parallel, marginally easier line to the Northeast Buttress up the same 5,000-ft face, first climbed in 1951 with a 1957 variation start; mostly unroped 3rd/4th-class climbing through a 'dangerous jungle gym' of vertical brush, with a sustained roughly 700-ft crux rock band.

wa_bonanza_peak_northeast_buttress.overview: Bonanza Peak is the highest non-volcanic summit in Washington. This route is the Northeast Buttress, a serious, mostly-rock alpine line that gains Bonanza's true (9,516') summit directly, branching off the standard Mary Green Glacier approach at about 8,350 ft. Graded V, 5.7/5.8, the Northeast Buttress offers sustained, exposed ridge climbing on generally solid but lichen-covered rock, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness above Holden and Lake Chelan.
